citations.quote:
Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
for $x\in H$ and finite $F\subseteq I$ put

$$P_Fx:=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i .$$

Then the following four assertions are equivalent:

1. **(completeness)** the closed linear span of $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is $H$;
2. **(zero complement)** the only vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is $0$;
3. **(Parseval)** $\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}|\langle x,e_i\rangle|^2=\|x\|^2$
   for every $x\in H$, the sum being the supremum of the finite subsums
   ([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]);
4. **(net convergence)** the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$
   converges to $x$ for every $x\in H$.

Assertion 2 is the statement
$\operatorname{span}\{e_i : i\in I\}^\perp=\{0\}$
([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]).

derivations.claim: [One inclusion] Let $x\in D(A)$ with coefficients $c_n=\langle x,e_n\rangle$ satisfy $Ax=\lambda x$. By [F1] both series $\sum_n\lambda_nc_ne_n$ and $\sum_n\lambda c_ne_n$ converge, so their difference $\sum_n(\lambda_n-\lambda)c_ne_n=0$ converges; its coefficients in the orthonormal family are $(\lambda_n-\lambda)c_n$, and by the uniqueness of coefficients in [F2] all of them vanish. Hence $c_n=0$ whenever $\lambda_n\ne\lambda$, so $x=\sum_{n:\lambda_n=\lambda}c_ne_n$ lies in the closed linear span of $\{e_n:\lambda_n=\lambda\}$.

[The converse inclusion] Conversely let $I:=\{n:\lambda_n=\lambda\}$ and let $x=\sum_{n\in I}c_ne_n$ be an element of the closed linear span of $\{e_n:n\in I\}$, so that $\sum_{n\in I}|c_n|^2<\infty$ and the series converges by [F2]. Then $\sum_n\lambda_n^2|\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2=\sum_{n\in I}\lambda^2|c_n|^2<\infty$, so $x\in D(A)$ by [F1], and $Ax=\sum_{n\in I}\lambda c_ne_n=\lambda x$.

[Clause (a)] Steps 1.1 and 1.2 give $\ker(A-\lambda I)=\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{e_n:\lambda_n=\lambda\}$ for every real $\lambda$, and this span is nonzero exactly when $\lambda\in\{\lambda_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ because $e_n\ne0$.

[Clause (b)] Assume the $\lambda_n$ are pairwise distinct and let $\lambda=\lambda_k$. Then $\{n:\lambda_n=\lambda\}=\{k\}$, so step 2.1 gives $\ker(A-\lambda_kI)=\mathbb Ce_k$; every such eigenspace is one-dimensional with eigenvector $e_k
e0$, and distinct eigenspaces are orthogonal because $\langle e_m,e_kangle=0$ for $m
e k$ by [F2]. If $x
e0$ satisfies $Ax=\lambda x$, then $\lambda=\lambda_k$ for some $k$ by step 2.1 and $x\in\mathbb Ce_k$; conversely every nonzero multiple of $e_k$ is an eigenvector by [F1].

[Clause (c)] The span of the union of the eigenspaces contains every $e_n$, hence contains $D_0=\operatorname{span}\{e_n\}$, which is dense in $H$ by [F1]; therefore the span of the eigenspaces is dense.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.2 allows the index set $I=\{n:\lambda_n=\lambda\}$ to be empty, in which case the sum $\sum_{n\in I}c_ne_n$ is $0$; step 2.1 then gives $\ker(A-\lambda I)=\overline{\operatorname{span}}\varnothing=\{0\}$, so $\lambda$ is not an eigenvalue, as clause (a) states.
Step 1.1 allows $x=0$ in $D(A)$: the zero vector lies in every eigenspace, and step 3.1 extracts the eigenvalue only from a nonzero eigenvector, matching the nonzero-multiple clause (b).
Step 3.1: for pairwise distinct eigenvalues and $\lambda=\lambda_k$ the carrier set is the singleton $\{k\}$, and clause (b) reads $\ker(A-\lambda_kI)=\mathbb Ce_k$.

Step 3.1 applies only under the pairwise-distinct hypothesis; clause (a) retains the closed span of all carriers, so repeated eigenvalues $\lambda_m=\lambda_n$ are covered without claiming one-dimensionality.

boundaries.reason: The statement is about a fixed orthonormal family and an arbitrary fixed real $\lambda$; no interval, endpoint value or one-sided limit occurs, and $\{\lambda_n\}$ need not be discrete.

boundaries.evidence: The Axiom of Countable Choice is assumed in the statement and used through [F1] and [F2]; steps 1.1-4.1 invoke no further choice.
Step 1.1: if $Ax=\lambda x$ with $x\ne0$, the coefficient expansion of $x$ over the carriers shows $x\in\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{e_n:\lambda_n=\lambda\}$.
Step 1.2: conversely every element of the closed span of the carriers is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $\lambda$, so the equality of clause (a) is a genuine equivalence.

risk_review.notes: Read all five steps and diagonal adjoint/core supplier proof. Coefficient uniqueness proves both inclusions; on the matching-index subspace the weighted domain sum is lambda squared times the ordinary square sum. Empty matching set gives {0}, lambda=0 is admissible, distinct values give exactly scalar multiples; density follows from completeness. Countable Choice is stated. citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on the
measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on the complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be
$\Sigma$-measurable. Put
$$D(f(E)):=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_X|f|^2\,dE_x<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,$$
where the scalar measures $E_x$ are those of
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]], and for $x\in D(f(E))$ set
$$f(E)x:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi_E\bigl(f\,\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}\bigr)x,$$
For $H\ne\{0\}$, the bounded integrals $\Phi_E$ are those of
[[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], and the limit is taken in the norm of $H$.
For $H=\{0\}$, define $\Phi_E(g)$ to be the unique operator on $H$ for every bounded measurable $g$. Then $E_0$ is the zero measure, $D(f(E))=H$, and $f(E)0=0$. Thus this case is defined directly without applying a theorem requiring a nonzero space.

**Well-definedness.** $D(f(E))$ is a linear subspace: the estimate
$E_{x+y}\le2E_x+2E_y$ for scalar measures and $E_{\alpha x}=|\alpha|^2E_x$
follow from $\|E(B)(x+y)\|^2\le2\|E(B)x\|^2+2\|E(B)y\|^2$ and
$\|E(B)\alpha x\|^2=|\alpha|^2\|E(B)x\|^2$. Writing $f_n:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}$
the sets $\{|f|\le n\}$ are measurable, so $f_n$ is bounded and measurable.
For $m,n\ge N$,
$$|f_n-f_m|^2\le |f|^2\mathbf1_{\{|f|>N\}}.$$
The integral of the right side against $E_x$ tends to zero by
[[thm-dominated-convergence]], with the integrable majorant $|f|^2$ and
pointwise limit zero since $f$ is finite-valued. Linearity of the bounded
calculus ([[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]]) and its quadratic identity give
$$\|\Phi_E(f_n)x-\Phi_E(f_m)x\|^2=\int|f_n-f_m|^2\,dE_x.$$
These clauses hold directly on the zero space as well. Hence the truncation
vectors are Cauchy and converge uniquely by Hilbert-space completeness
([[def-hilbert-space]]). The limit is linear in $x$ because every truncation
operator is linear and addition and scalar multiplication are norm-continuous.
Countable Choice is inherited from the bounded PVM suppliers; no further
choice is needed to take these specified limits.

Finally, if two $\Sigma$-measurable functions $f,g$ agree outside a measurable
set $N$ with $E(N)=0$, then $E_x(N)=\|E(N)x\|^2=0$ for every $x$. Thus the
integrals of $|f|^2$ and $|g|^2$ agree, so their domains agree. At every
truncation level their bounded truncations agree outside $N$; the quadratic
identity applied to the difference gives equal truncation vectors for every
$x$. Taking limits gives $f(E)x=g(E)x$ on their common domain.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$,
and for $x,y\in H$ define

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad E_{x,y}(B):=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle \qquad(B\in\Sigma).$$

Then:

1. $E_x$ is a positive measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ with $E_x(X)=\|x\|^2$ and
   $0\le E_x(B)\le\|x\|^2$ for every $B$;
2. $E_{x,y}$ is a finite complex measure on $(X,\Sigma)$, the map
   $(x,y)\mapsto E_{x,y}$ is linear in $x$ and conjugate-linear in $y$, and
   $E_{y,x}=\overline{E_{x,y}}$, meaning $E_{y,x}(B)=\overline{E_{x,y}(B)}$ for
   every $B$;
3. $|E_{x,y}|(X)\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$, so $|E_{x,y}(B)|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$ for every
   $B$, and the polarization identity
   $$E_{x,y}=\frac14\sum_{k=0}^{3}i^kE_{x+i^ky}$$
   holds as an identity of complex measures, where $i^k$ are the fourth roots
   of unity $1,i,-1,-i$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ and spectrum $\sigma(A)$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]). Then:

(a) $E_A(\mathbb R\setminus\sigma(A))=0$, equivalently $E_A(B)=E_A(B\cap\sigma(A))$ for every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$; and $E_A(U)\ne0$ for every nonempty relatively open subset $U\subseteq\sigma(A)$. Thus the support of $E_A$ is exactly $\sigma(A)$.

(b) For every density operator $\rho$ on $H$, the scalar law $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_A(B))$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (b) satisfies
$$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)=\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B\cap\sigma(A))\qquad\text{and}\qquad \mu^{A}_{\rho}(\sigma(A))=1$$
for every Borel set $B$: no mass lies outside the spectrum.

(c) More generally, if $C\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a Borel set with $E_A(C)=0$, then $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(C)=0$ for every density operator $\rho$, and if $E_A(C)=E_A(\mathbb R)$ then $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(C)=1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: [The inverse is a linear isometry] Since $U$ is bijective, $U^{-1}$ exists; it is linear because $U$ is linear. For $a=Ux$ and $b=Uy$ in $K$, $\langle U^{-1}a,U^{-1}b\rangle_H=\langle x,y\rangle_H=\langle Ux,Uy\rangle_K=\langle a,b\rangle_K$; hence $U^{-1}$ is isometric, and so is $U$, so $\|Ux\|_K=\|x\|_H$ for every $x\in H$.

[$E$ is a projection-valued measure] For a Borel set $B$ define $E(B):=UE_T(B)U^{-1}\in\mathcal B(K)$. It is an orthogonal projection: $E(B)^2=UE_T(B)U^{-1}UE_T(B)U^{-1}=E(B)$ and $\langle E(B)a,b\rangle_K=\langle E_T(B)U^{-1}a,U^{-1}b\rangle_H=\langle U^{-1}a,E_T(B)U^{-1}b\rangle_H=\langle a,E(B)b\rangle_K$ for all $a,b\in K$, using the isometry of $U^{-1}$ and the self-adjointness of $E_T(B)$. Moreover $E(\varnothing)=0$, $E(\mathbb R)=I$, $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$, and for pairwise disjoint $B_n$ with union $B$, $\bigl\|E(B)a-\sum_{n\le N}E(B_n)a\bigr\|_K=\bigl\|E_T(B)U^{-1}a-\sum_{n\le N}E_T(B_n)U^{-1}a\bigr\|_H\to0$ by [F2]. Hence $E$ is a projection-valued measure on the Borel sets of $\mathbb R$.

[$T'$ is well defined, linear and symmetric] If $Ux=Ux'$ then $x=x'$ by injectivity, so $T'(Ux):=U(Tx)$ is well defined; $D(T')=U D(T)$ is a linear subspace, dense because $D(T)$ is dense and $U$ is bijective, and $T'$ is linear because $T$ and $U$ are. For $x,y\in D(T)$, using the isometry of $U$ in both directions and the self-adjointness of $T$, $\langle T'Ux,Uy\rangle_K=\langle UTx,Uy\rangle_K=\langle Tx,y\rangle_H=\langle x,Ty\rangle_H=\langle Ux,UTy\rangle_K=\langle Ux,T'Uy\rangle_K$.

[$E$ is regular with transported scalar measures] For $y,z\in K$ and Borel $B$, $E_{y,z}(B):=\langle E(B)y,z\rangle_K=\langle E_T(B)U^{-1}y,U^{-1}z\rangle_H=E_{T,U^{-1}y,U^{-1}z}(B)$ by the isometry of $U^{-1}$ and the definition of $E$; in particular $E_y(B)=E_{T,U^{-1}y}(B)$ with $U^{-1}y\in H$. Since $E_T$ is regular, each $E_{T,x}$ is a regular Borel measure [F2], so each scalar measure $E_y$ of $E$ is regular and $E$ is regular.

[$T'$ is self-adjoint] Let $y'\in D((T')^*)$, put $z:=U^{-1}y'\in H$, $w:=(T')^*y'\in K$ and $v:=U^{-1}w\in H$. For every $x\in D(T)$, $\langle Tx,z\rangle_H=\langle UTx,y'\rangle_K=\langle T'Ux,y'\rangle_K=\langle Ux,w\rangle_K=\langle x,v\rangle_H$ by the isometry of $U^{-1}$; hence the functional $x\mapsto\langle Tx,z\rangle_H$ is bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_H)$ by $\|v\|_H\|x\|_H$, so $z\in D(T^*)=D(T)$ and $Tz=v$ by [F4]. Therefore $y'=Uz\in U D(T)=D(T')$ and $(T')^*y'=w=Uv=UTz=T'y'$; thus $D((T')^*)\subseteq D(T')$, and with step 2.2 and [F4] the operator $T'$ is self-adjoint.

[$E$ represents $T'$] Let $y\in D(T')$, that is $x:=U^{-1}y\in D(T)$. By [F1] applied to $T$ at $x$, $\int\lambda^2\,dE_{T,x}<\infty$ and $\int\lambda\,dE_T(\lambda)x=Tx$; by step 3.1 with $y=z$, $E_y=E_{T,x}$, so $\int\lambda^2\,dE_y<\infty$ and $\int\lambda\,dE_y=\int\lambda\,dE_{T,x}$. Conversely, if $\int\lambda^2\,dE_y<\infty$ for some $y\in K$, then step 3.1 gives $\int\lambda^2\,dE_{T,U^{-1}y}<\infty$, so $U^{-1}y\in D(T)$ by [F1] and $y\in U D(T)=D(T')$. Thus $D(T')=\{y\in K:\int\lambda^2\,dE_y(\lambda)<\infty\}$, the exact domain of the unbounded integral $S:=\int\lambda\,dE(\lambda)$ against the projection-valued measure $E$. For $y\in D(T')$ and every $z\in K$, $\langle Sy,z\rangle_K=\int\lambda\,dE_{y,z}(\lambda)=\int\lambda\,dE_{T,U^{-1}y,U^{-1}z}(\lambda)=\langle TU^{-1}y,U^{-1}z\rangle_H=\langle T'y,z\rangle_K$, the middle equality by [F1] applied to $T$ at $U^{-1}y\in D(T)$; since the pairings separate points of $K$, $Sy=T'y$. By the converse clause of [F1] applied to $S=T'$ and the regular projection-valued measure $E$, the measure $E$ is the spectral projection-valued measure of $T'$.

[Clause (c)] For $x\in H$, $E(B)Ux=UE_T(B)U^{-1}Ux=UE_T(B)x$, so $\|E(B)Ux\|_K^2=\|E_T(B)x\|_H^2$ by the isometry of $U$; for unit $x$ this is the asserted identity of scalar laws, both sides being the values at $B$ of the positive measures $E_{Ux}$ and $E_{T,x}$ of [F2].

[Clause (d)] By [F3] applied to $T$, $\sigma(T)$ is the support of $E_T$; by step 4.1 the measure $E$ is the spectral projection-valued measure of $T'$, so [F3] applied to $T'$ shows that $\sigma(T')$ is the support of $E$. For every Borel $B$, $E(B)=0$ if and only if $E_T(B)=0$, because $U$ and $U^{-1}$ are bijective; hence $E$ and $E_T$ have the same null sets and the same nonempty relatively open subsets on which they fail to vanish, so their supports -- and therefore $\sigma(T')$ and $\sigma(T)$ -- coincide.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 carries the empty Borel set: $E(\varnothing)=UE_T(\varnothing)U^{-1}=0$ and $E(\mathbb R)=I$.
Step 2.2 uses injectivity of $U$ to make $T'$ well defined, so the zero vector lies in $D(T')$ with $T'0=0$; step 3.2 computes the adjoint there without exception.
The construction is applied once to the single pair $(T,E_T)$; steps 2.1-5.1 are uniform in the operator, so the single-operator case is the statement.
The zero operator is included: step 2.1 gives $E(B)=UE_T(B)U^{-1}$ with $E_T(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\})=0$, and step 4.1 gives $T'=0$ on $D(T')=K$; step 5.1 transports $\sigma(T)=\{0\}$.

boundaries.reason: The transport is at the level of Borel sets and spectral integrals; no interval endpoint, boundary value or one-sided limit is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are assumed for the spectral theorem [F1] and the scalar-measure lemma [F2]; steps 3.2, 4.1 use them only through those suppliers.

boundaries.reason: Clauses (a)-(d) assert the constructed objects and identities (self-adjointness, the integral representation, equality of spectra); no biconditional is asserted, so there is no forward direction to check.
As no biconditional is asserted in clauses (a)-(d), there is no reverse direction; the uniqueness of $E$ is inherited from the spectral theorem [F1] cited in step 4.1.

risk_review.notes: Read all eight steps and actual PVM, unbounded integral, adjoint, spectral theorem and spectral-support supplier statements; read the support proof. Unitary conjugation preserves adjoint domains, strong additivity and scalar regularity, and equality of scalar measures preserves the exact integral domain. Pairing equality identifies the integral action. The support supplier requires a nonzero space: when H={0}, K={0}, every projection and integral is the unique zero operator and every complex resolvent parameter is invertible on {0}, so both spectra are empty directly. For nonzero spaces the cited support argument applies. No reader/refuter finding targets this carrier; no new Choice use beyond declared suppliers.

citations.quote:
**(a) Adopted framework assumptions.** Adopt the state and composition postulate P1, the observable and probability postulate P2, the autonomous-dynamics postulate P4 and the kinematics and massive-particle model postulate P5, in the readings of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]], [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]], [[def-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-framework-evolution]] and [[def-nrqm-kinematics-framework-massive-spin-s-model]] ([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]], [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]], [[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]], [[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]]). Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix real model parameters $m>0$ (mass parameter, unit $\mathrm{kg}$), $\omega>0$ (angular frequency, unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$) and the action constant $\hbar>0$ (unit $\mathrm J\,\mathrm s$) of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]] clause (d)4, and put
$$\ell:=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{m\omega}}>0\qquad\text{(unit }\mathrm m\text{),}$$
the model's length scale.

**(b) One-dimensional realization.** Write $\mathcal H_1:=L^{2}(\mathbb R,dx;\mathbb C)$ for the model's one-dimensional state space, the complex Hilbert space of almost-everywhere classes with inner product linear in the first argument, taken in the scalar reading $r=1$ of the component-valued space of [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] for $d=1$. The model's **position** and **momentum** are the operators of that lemma at $d=1$, $r=1$, namely
$$Q:=M_x,\qquad D(Q)=\{f\in\mathcal H_1:xf\in L^{2}\},\qquad (Qf)(x)=xf(x),$$
$$P:=-i\hbar D_x,\qquad D(P)=\{f\in\mathcal H_1:\text{the weak derivative }D_xf\text{ lies in }L^{2}\},\qquad Pf=-i\hbar D_xf,$$
which are densely defined and self-adjoint with exactly these domains; the model assigns to $(Q,\mathrm m)$ and to $(P,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1})$ the status of assigned sharp observables in the sense of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (a), with outcome laws read from P2.

**(c) Energy and excitation-number observables.** Let $g_0,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ and the unitary $D:L^{2}(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^{2}(\mathbb R,dx)$ be the Hermite data and scaling map of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]] clauses (a), (b) for the parameters $m,\omega,\hbar$. Put $\mathscr P_y:=\{p g_0:p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^{2}(\mathbb R,dy)$; the Hermite recurrence [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] identifies this polynomial-Gaussian space with $\operatorname{span}\{g_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$, and its scaled image $\mathscr P_x:=D(\mathscr P_y)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ is the core supplied by the scaling theorem. Let $A$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the family $(g_n)$ and eigenvalues $2n+1$. The model's **energy operator** is
$$H_1:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,D A D^{-1},\qquad D(H_1):=\{f\in\mathcal H_1:D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$
the operator of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]] clause (b); its exact domain, action, spectrum and eigenbasis are those established there. The model assigns to $(H_1,\mathrm J)$ the status of assigned energy observable of the isolated system in the sense of [[def-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-framework-evolution]] clauses (a) and (b): the model's flow is $U(t)=\exp(-itH_1/\hbar)$ and the model's Schroedinger dynamics is the one of that definition. Let $N$ be the self-adjoint number operator on $L^{2}(\mathbb R,dy)$ of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-closed-ladder-domains]] for the Hermite family $(g_n)$, and set $N_\psi:=DND^{-1}$. Its transported domain and action are
$$D(N_\psi)=\Bigl\{f\in\mathcal H_1:\sum_n n^2|\langle f,\psi_n\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad N_\psi f=\sum_n n\langle f,\psi_n\rangle\psi_n,$$
with the series converging in $\mathcal H_1$; it is self-adjoint by [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-unitary-transport-of-spectral-pvms]] clauses (a), (d). The model assigns to $(N_\psi,1/\mathrm{count})$ the status of its dimensionless excitation-number observable; here $\mathrm{count}$ denotes one excitation count and is dimensionless, so the spectral coordinate $n$ records $n$ excitations, and its outcome laws are read by P2. On the scaled polynomial-Gaussian core $\mathscr P_x$ the operator $H_1$ is the self-adjoint realization of the quadratic expression: for every $f\in\mathscr P_x$,
$$H_1f=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^{2}}{2}x^{2}f$$
pointwise, and for every $f\in D(H_1)$ the weak identity $\int (H_1f)\varphi\,dx=\int f\bigl(-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\varphi''+\frac{m\omega^{2}}{2}x^{2}\varphi\bigr)dx$ holds for every $\varphi\in C_c^{\infty}(\mathbb R)$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]] clauses (c), (d)). The formal differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\frac{d^{2}}{dx^{2}}+\frac{m\omega^{2}}{2}x^{2}$ is the model's **quadratic potential energy plus kinetic energy** reading; no identification of $D(H_1)$ with any independently defined maximal differential-operator domain, and no separate quadratic-form-domain characterization, is asserted.

**(d) Three-dimensional isotropic realization.** For the spinless reading $s=0$ of the massive-particle model of [[def-nrqm-kinematics-framework-massive-spin-s-model]], with state space $\mathcal H_3:=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3},dx;\mathbb C)$, position operators $Q_j$ and momentum operators $P_k$ ($j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) with the domains and units of that definition, the model with common frequency $\omega$ has **energy operator** $H_3$ equal to the diagonal operator $H$ of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-multidimensional-oscillator-completeness]] clause (c) for $d=3$, $m_j=m$, $\omega_j=\omega$, a self-adjoint operator on $\mathcal H_3$ with the domain, spectrum and core displayed there. The model assigns to $(H_3,\mathrm J)$ the status of assigned energy observable in the reading of clause (c); its eigenbasis and the identity $H_3=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\bigl(-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\partial_{x_j}^{2}+\frac{m\omega^{2}}{2}x_j^{2}\bigr)$ on the core are those of that theorem, and the one-dimensional realization of clauses (b) and (c) is the coordinate specialization of this one.

**(e) Physical reading and scope.** Clause (c) defines the model quantities that the page calls the energy and excitation number; it is a **model assumption** that the energy of the declared isolated particle is the assigned observable $(H_1,\mathrm J)$ and that $(N_\psi,1/\mathrm{count})$ is its excitation-number observable. The additive constant of the potential energy is removed at the minimum: for a one-dimensional potential-energy function $V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$, with values in joules for position $x$ in metres, suppose $V$ has a non-degenerate local minimum at $0$, meaning $V'(0)=0$ and $V''(0)>0$. Taylor's theorem gives $V(x)-V(0)=\frac{1}{2}V''(0)x^{2}+o(x^{2})$ as $x\to0$; the oscillator model approximates this shifted potential-energy function by its quadratic term and sets $m\omega^{2}=V''(0)$. The oscillator's quantum ground energy in this convention is $\hbar\omega/2$. With only the stated $C^2$ regularity, the remainder is $o(x^2)$; no quantitative finite-amplitude error bound is asserted on this page (Binney §3.1, cited in the references). No measured value, no laboratory identification and no derivation of $m$ or $\omega$ from any microscopic or environmental theory is asserted. The model contains no damping, no external driving, no time-dependent parameters, no coupling to electromagnetic fields or radiation, no spin-dependent force, no anharmonic term, no relativistic correction and no boundary or many-body effect; those are separate model assumptions belonging to their own items. The parameters $m$ and $\omega$ are model parameters of dimensions $\mu$ and $\tau^{-1}$ in the conventions of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]], and all displayed quantities are read in the units fixed there.

**(f) Status.** Clauses (a)-(e) fix the objects used by the theorems of this page and record the readings of P1, P2, P4 and P5 in the model's terminology. They assert no preparation or apparatus model, no detection model, no joint outcome law of position and momentum and no empirical result.

**(a) Assigned sharp observables.** Adopt the observable and probability postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]] (P2) for a declared system whose state space is the model's [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. An **assigned sharp observable** of the system is a pair $(A,u_A)$ consisting of a densely defined self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\subset H\to H$ on the assigned Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]], [[def-hilbert-space]]) and a **declared unit** $u_A$ in which the real spectral coordinate of $A$ is read, in the sense of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. The domain $D(A)$ is part of the assignment: symmetry on a smaller domain, or a formal differential expression, does not by itself supply an assigned observable ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). Whether a concrete laboratory quantity of a given apparatus is described by a particular pair $(A,u_A)$ is a tested identification with uncertainty under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7 and is not produced by this definition.

**(b) Spectral measure and outcome law.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of the cited spectral suppliers. The self-adjoint operator $A$ has a unique spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$, with $D(A)=\{x:\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{A,x}<\infty\}$ and $Ax=\int\lambda\,dE_A(\lambda)x$, where $E_{A,x}(B)=\langle E_A(B)x,x\rangle$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For a preparation $\rho$, that is a state $\rho\in D(H)$ of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]], the **outcome law** of the pair $(A,u_A)$ in the preparation $\rho$ is the assignment
$$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_A(B)\bigr)\qquad(B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel}),$$
the reading of clause (ii) of P2; for the pure preparation $[\psi]$ of a unit vector $\psi$ it is $\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_A(B)\psi\|^{2}$, which depends only on the ray by [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]. The law is a probability measure on the Borel sets by [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (b), and it is affine in the preparation: for a statistical mixture $\sum_nw_n\rho_n$ one has $\mu^{A}_{\sum_nw_n\rho_n}=\sum_nw_n\mu^{A}_{\rho_n}$ by [[lem-nrqm-observables-outcome-law-affinity-and-trace-norm-continuity]] clause (b).

**(c) Outcome sets and exact values.** A declared finite-resolution outcome of the quantity is a Borel set $B$; its probability in the preparation $\rho$ is $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)$, and a "value in $B$" is read only through this number. The reading of an **exact value** $\lambda$ is the singleton $B=\{\lambda\}$, with probability $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})$; by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-measure-atoms-and-eigenvalues]] clauses (a) and (b) this number is zero for every preparation unless $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$, and when $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue it is the total weight of the eigenspace. In particular the model provides no normalizable eigenvector at a non-eigenvalue of $A$, and an exact value of a quantity with no eigenvalues is an idealization outside the assignment, in the sense of clause (iii) of P2.

**(d) Spectral support.** The outcomes of the observable lie in its spectrum: with $\sigma(A)$ the spectrum of [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]], one has $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)=\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B\cap\sigma(A))$ and $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\sigma(A))=1$ for every preparation by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-support-and-outcome-law]] clause (b). This is the precise reading of the statement that the result of a measurement lies in the spectrum of the observable.

**(e) Moments.** The **mean** and the **variance** of the outcome law in a preparation are the numbers $\int\lambda\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ and $\int(\lambda-m)^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ with $m$ the mean, read in the declared unit $u_A$ and its square respectively; they exist only under the integrability hypotheses of [[lem-nrqm-observables-moments-and-variance]], which also supplies the formulas in terms of $A$ and the state. For a pure preparation of a unit vector $\psi\in D(A)$ the mean and the second moment are $\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle$ and $\|A\psi\|^{2}$; membership of $\psi$ in $D(A)$ or in $D(A^{2})$ is a genuine hypothesis and is not asserted for an arbitrary preparation.

**(f) Unsharp finite outcomes are separate.** Clause (iv) of P2 permits a finite family of bounded effects $F_a$ with $0\le F_a\le I$ and $\sum_aF_a=I$ and outcome probabilities $\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)$ as an operational description of a finite-resolution apparatus. That extension is tied to an apparatus instrument and is developed, together with state updates, on the measurement-and-instruments page; this definition fixes only the sharp outcome law of clause (b) and makes no claim that every laboratory procedure realizes it.

**(g) Status.** Clauses (a)-(f) record the readings of P1 and P2 in the vocabulary of this page and fix the terminology used by the later pages of the category. They adopt no physical assumption beyond P1 and P2 and the choice hypotheses of the spectral theorem, assert no dynamics, no joint measurement of several observables, no detector realization and no empirical result, and make no claim that any physical system is exactly described by an assigned pair $(A,u_A)$. The additive additivity, support, atom and moment statements cited are mathematical consequences proved in the cited items; their physical reading is exactly the reading of P2 fixed here.

**(a) Assigned energy observable.** Adopt the autonomous-dynamics postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]] (P4) for a declared isolated system whose state space is the model's [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. An **assigned energy observable** of the system is an assigned sharp observable $(H_{\mathrm{op}},u_H)$ in the sense of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (a), whose declared unit $u_H$ is an energy unit in the sense of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]] (joules in the SI conventions fixed there). Thus $H_{\mathrm{op}}:D(H_{\mathrm{op}})\subset H\to H$ is densely defined and self-adjoint ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), with spectral projection-valued measure $E_H$ on the Borel sets of $\mathbb R$ under the choice hypotheses of [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]] ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and its outcome law in a preparation is the law of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (b). The assignment of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ is part of the model specification, as in clause (i) of P4; this definition asserts nothing about which laboratory quantity of a concrete system realizes it.

**(b) The unitary flow.** The **time evolution** or **flow** of the isolated system is the family
$$U(t):=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tH_{\mathrm{op}}\Bigr):=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}\,dE_H(\lambda)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),$$
the reading of clause (ii) of P4 in the spectral calculus of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ ([[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]); here $\hbar>0$ is the reduced Planck constant with its value and unit fixed by [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]], so that $tH_{\mathrm{op}}/\hbar$ is dimensionless. Equivalently, $U(t)=e^{itT}$ for the self-adjoint generator $T:=-H_{\mathrm{op}}/\hbar$ with $D(T)=D(H_{\mathrm{op}})$; the two readings agree by the uniqueness of the generator in Stone's theorem, and by [[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]] ([[lem-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-flow-calculus]] clause (a)) the family $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group: $U(0)=I$, $U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)$, $U(t)^{*}=U(t)^{-1}=U(-t)$ ([[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]).

**(c) Schroedinger picture.** The **Schroedinger-picture evolution** of a preparation is fixed by clause (iii) of P4. A state vector evolves by $\psi(t):=U(t)\psi(0)$ for every $\psi(0)\in H$, and the **state at time $t$** of the pure preparation $[\psi(0)]$ is the pure preparation $[\psi(t)]$, which is well defined because $U(t)$ is injective; a general preparation $\rho$, that is an element of the state space $D(H)$ of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]], evolves by
$$\rho(t):=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^{*},$$
the reading of clause (iii) of P4 in the density-operator vocabulary of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]] ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]). In this picture the assigned observables are held fixed at their assigned values and the preparation moves.

**(d) Heisenberg picture.** For a **bounded** assigned sharp observable $(A,u_A)$ — that is, an assigned sharp observable with $A\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), so that $A$ is self-adjoint and everywhere defined — the **Heisenberg representative** of $(A,u_A)$ at time $t$ is the pair $(A_H(t),u_A)$ with the same declared unit and
$$A_H(t):=U(t)^{*}AU(t)=U(-t)AU(t).$$
By [[lem-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-heisenberg-flow]] clauses (a) and (d), $A_H(t)$ is again bounded and self-adjoint with spectral projection-valued measure $E_{A_H(t)}(B)=U(-t)E_A(B)U(t)$, so $(A_H(t),u_A)$ is again an assigned sharp observable of the framework; in this picture the preparation is held fixed at its value at time $0$ and the observables move. The two pictures are two bookkeeping devices for the same model; the statement that they assign the same outcome laws is proved in the Heisenberg-picture theorem of this page, not assumed here.

**(e) Stationary preparations.** A preparation $\rho\in D(H)$ is **stationary** for the assigned energy observable when $\rho(t)=\rho$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$. A pure preparation $[\psi]$ is stationary when $[\psi(t)]=[\psi(0)]$ for every $t$, that is, when the evolved vector remains in the ray of $\psi$; the characterization of this condition by the eigenrays of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ is proved in the stationary-states theorem of this page, not assumed here. An **energy eigenstate** is a pure preparation of a unit eigenvector of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$, and a **stationary state** in the model is a stationary pure preparation; by that theorem the two notions coincide.

**(f) Energy-compatible observables.** An assigned sharp observable $(A,u_A)$ is **compatible with the energy**, or **energy-compatible**, when its spectral projection-valued measure and that of the energy commute strongly,
$$E_A(B)E_H(C)=E_H(C)E_A(B)\qquad\text{for all Borel }B,C\subseteq\mathbb R .$$
This is an equality of bounded operators on $H$, not a relation between formal commutators on a small domain; the phrase **conserved quantity** for an energy-compatible assigned observable is a claim about the time invariance of its outcome law and is established in the energy-conservation theorem of this page for bounded $A$.

**(g) Status.** Clauses (a)-(f) record the readings of P4 together with P1 and P2 in the vocabulary of this page and fix the terminology used by the later pages of the category. They adopt no physical assumption beyond P4, P1 and P2 and the choice hypotheses of the cited mathematics, assert no dynamics for a prescribed time-dependent family or for an open system (clauses (iv) and (v) of P4 are separate model assumptions treated on their own pages), assert no measurement model, no apparatus realization and no empirical result, and make no claim that any laboratory system is exactly isolated.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a complete orthonormal family of $H$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), let $(\lambda_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subseteq\mathbb R$, and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]]:
$$D(A)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\sum_n\lambda_n^2|\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Ax=\sum_n\lambda_n\langle x,e_n\rangle e_n .$$
Then:

(a) for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ the eigenspace of $A$ at $\lambda$ is the closed linear span of the basis vectors carrying the eigenvalue $\lambda$:
$$\ker(A-\lambda I)=\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{e_n:\lambda_n=\lambda\};$$
in particular $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ exactly when $\lambda=\lambda_n$ for some $n$;

(b) if $\lambda_m\ne\lambda_n$ whenever $m\ne n$, then $\ker(A-\lambda_nI)=\mathbb Ce_n$ for every $n$: every eigenspace is one-dimensional with eigenvector $e_n$, the eigenspaces are pairwise orthogonal, and every nonzero eigenvector of $A$ is a nonzero multiple of some $e_n$;

(c) in the situation of (b) the linear span of all eigenspaces of $A$ is $\operatorname{span}\{e_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$, which is dense in $H$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $E_{A,x}(B):=\langle E_A(B)x,x\rangle$ be its scalar measures ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]). For $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ say that $\lambda$ is an **eigenvalue** of $A$ when $Ax=\lambda x$ for some nonzero $x\in D(A)$, the domain-restricted reading of [[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]. Then:

(a) The orthogonal projection $E_A(\{\lambda\})$ is the projection of $H$ onto the eigenspace $\ker(A-\lambda)=\{x\in D(A):Ax=\lambda x\}$; in particular $E_A(\{\lambda\})\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$.

(b) For every density operator $\rho$ on $H$, that is every self-adjoint positive trace-class $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)), the number $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_{A}(\{\lambda\}))$ is the weight that the scalar law $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ assigns to the singleton $\{\lambda\}$: it vanishes for every $\rho$ whenever $\lambda$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$, and it equals $1$ for the pure state $T_{u,u}$ of every unit eigenvector $u\in\ker(A-\lambda)$.

(c) If $A$ has no eigenvalues at all, then $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})=0$ for every density operator $\rho$ and every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$: the scalar law of every state carries no point mass, while its values on general Borel sets remain $\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_{A}(B))$.

Clauses (a)-(c) are mathematical statements about $A$, $E_A$ and the density operators; no physical interpretation of $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ is asserted here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ and spectrum $\sigma(A)$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]). Then:

(a) $E_A(\mathbb R\setminus\sigma(A))=0$, equivalently $E_A(B)=E_A(B\cap\sigma(A))$ for every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$; and $E_A(U)\ne0$ for every nonempty relatively open subset $U\subseteq\sigma(A)$. Thus the support of $E_A$ is exactly $\sigma(A)$.

(b) For every density operator $\rho$ on $H$, the scalar law $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_A(B))$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (b) satisfies
$$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)=\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B\cap\sigma(A))\qquad\text{and}\qquad \mu^{A}_{\rho}(\sigma(A))=1$$
for every Borel set $B$: no mass lies outside the spectrum.

(c) More generally, if $C\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a Borel set with $E_A(C)=0$, then $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(C)=0$ for every density operator $\rho$, and if $E_A(C)=E_A(\mathbb R)$ then $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(C)=1$.

Adopt the state and composition postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]] (P1) and the observable and probability postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]] (P2), and assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of the spectral suppliers. Let $H$ be the state space assigned to a declared system, let $(A,u_A)$ be an assigned sharp observable of the framework with spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ and spectrum $\sigma(A)$, and let $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ be the outcome law of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]]. Then for every preparation $\rho$ ([[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]) and every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$:

(a) **Probability measure.** $0\le\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)\le1$ and $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\mathbb R)=1$; for pairwise disjoint Borel sets $B_n$ with union $B$ one has $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)=\sum_n\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B_n)$; and for the pure preparation of a unit vector $\psi$ the law is $\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_A(B)\psi\|^{2}$. The declared outcome law of the model is therefore a probability measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$, not a formal weight attached to eigenvectors.

(b) **Mixtures.** If $\rho=\sum_nw_n\rho_n$ is a statistical mixture of preparations with weights $w_n\ge0$, $\sum_nw_n=1$, then $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)=\sum_nw_n\mu^{A}_{\rho_n}(B)$ for every Borel $B$, the series converging absolutely: the outcome law of a mixture is the weighted average of the outcome laws, with classical weights.

(c) **Exact values.** For $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ the probability of the exact value $\lambda$ is $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_A(\{\lambda\}))$; it is zero for every preparation whenever $\lambda$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$, and when $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue it equals the trace weight of the eigenspace $\ker(A-\lambda)$, with $\mu^{A}_{T_{u,u}}(\{\lambda\})=1$ for every unit eigenvector $u$.

(d) **Spectral support.** $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)=\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B\cap\sigma(A))$ and $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\sigma(A))=1$: outcomes outside the spectrum of the observable have probability zero.

(e) **No density and no discreteness are asserted.** The postulate asserts that $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ is a probability measure on the Borel sets and does not assert that it is a density with respect to Lebesgue measure or a finite or countable sum of point masses; the operational object named there is the probability of a declared Borel set, such as a finite-resolution bin, not the value of a density at a point ([[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]] clause (iii)). Which structure a particular pair $(A,\rho)$ exhibits is a property of that pair and is not fixed by the adopted law.

(f) **What is not claimed.** No mean, variance or higher moment is asserted by this item; their existence is conditional and is treated separately. No claim is made about the joint statistics of two or more observables, about the state after the outcome, about the physical mechanism producing an outcome, or about any concrete apparatus. The statement is conditional on P1 and P2 and on the cited mathematics.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $d\ge1$. For each $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ put $K_j^y:=L^2(\mathbb R,dy_j)$ and take a copy $(g^{(j)}_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of the Hermite family of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $K_j^y$. Define the left-associated completed tensor products by $\mathcal K_1^y:=K_1^y$ and $\mathcal K_r^y:=\mathcal K_{r-1}^y\widehat\otimes K_r^y$ for $2\le r\le d$. Let $\Theta_y^{(1)}:K_1^y\to L^2(\mathbb R,dy_1)$ be the identity; recursively, for $2\le r\le d$, let

$$\Theta_y^{(r)}:=\Theta_{r-1,1}^y\circ\bigl(\Theta_y^{(r-1)}\otimes I_{K_r^y}\bigr):\mathcal K_r^y\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r,dy),$$

where $\Theta_{r-1,1}^y:L^2(\mathbb R^{r-1},dy)\widehat\otimes K_r^y\to L^2(\mathbb R^r,dy)$ is the two-factor Euclidean product unitary of [[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]], and $\Theta_y^{(r-1)}\otimes I_{K_r^y}$ is the bounded tensor map of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]. Thus $\Theta_y^{(r)}$ is a specified unitary, with $\Theta_y^{(r)}(u\otimes v)(y',y_r)=\Theta_y^{(r-1)}u(y')v(y_r)$ almost everywhere. For $N=(n_1,\dots,n_d)\in\mathbb N^d$, set $G_N^{y,1}:=g^{(1)}_{n_1}$ and recursively $G_N^{y,r}:=G_N^{y,r-1}\otimes g^{(r)}_{n_r}$; define $g_N:=\Theta_y^{(d)}G_N^{y,d}\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$.

Let $\varphi:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N^d$ list the multi-indices by increasing total degree $M=\sum_jn_j$ and, within each finite level, in lexicographic order. By [[thm-stars-and-bars]] each level is finite and the levels exhaust $\mathbb N^d$, so this specifies a bijection. All sums indexed by $\mathbb N^d$ below are taken in this order; nonnegative sums equivalently mean the supremum of finite subsums.

The functions $g_N$ have smooth product representatives from the recursive construction. These representatives are unique: a continuous difference that is nonzero at a point remains nonzero on a ball of positive Lebesgue measure. The coordinate derivatives in (b) and (c) are taken on these representatives and their scaled products.

Then:

(a) $(g_N)_{N\in\mathbb N^d}$ is a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$: $\langle g_N,g_M\rangle=\delta_{NM}$ and every $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$ has $f=\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}\langle f,g_N\rangle g_N$ with $\|f\|^2=\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}|\langle f,g_N\rangle|^2$, the sum being the supremum over finite subfamilies ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]);

(b) with the eigenvalues $\lambda_N:=\sum_{j=1}^d(2n_j+1)=2M+d$, $M:=\sum_jn_j$, let $A_d$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the enumerated family $e_m:=g_{\varphi(m)}$ and eigenvalue sequence $\lambda_{\varphi(m)}$. Then $A_d$ is self-adjoint with

$$A_dg_N=\lambda_Ng_N,\qquad D(A_d)=\Bigl\{f:\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}\lambda_N^2|\langle f,g_N\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \sigma(A_d)=\{2M+d:M\in\mathbb N\}$$

(the spectrum by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]); the algebraic span of the $g_N$ is a core, and on that span

$$A_d=\sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(-\partial_{y_j}^2+y_j^2\bigr)$$

as operators, the $j$-th summand acting in the $j$-th coordinate;

(c) for real $m_j,\omega_j,\hbar>0$ put $\ell_j:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m_j\omega_j)}$ and let $D_j:K_j^y\to K_j^x:=L^2(\mathbb R,dx_j)$ be the one-dimensional unitary of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]]. Define $\mathcal K_1^x:=K_1^x$ and $\mathcal K_r^x:=\mathcal K_{r-1}^x\widehat\otimes K_r^x$ for $2\le r\le d$, and define $\Theta_x^{(1)}$ and $\Theta_x^{(r)}$ by the same recursion as $\Theta_y^{(r)}$, using the two-factor Euclidean product unitaries on the $x$-coordinate spaces. Let $\mathcal D_1:=D_1$ and recursively $\mathcal D_r:=\mathcal D_{r-1}\otimes D_r:\mathcal K_r^y\to\mathcal K_r^x$; each $\mathcal D_r$ is unitary by [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]. Put $D_d:=\Theta_x^{(d)}\mathcal D_d(\Theta_y^{(d)})^{-1}:L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R^d,dx)$. For $N\in\mathbb N^d$, define $G_N^{x,1}:=D_1g^{(1)}_{n_1}=:\psi^{(1)}_{n_1}$ and recursively $G_N^{x,r}:=G_N^{x,r-1}\otimes\psi^{(r)}_{n_r}$; then $\psi_N:=D_dg_N=\Theta_x^{(d)}G_N^{x,d}$. Let $H$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the enumerated family $\psi_{\varphi(m)}$ and eigenvalue sequence $E_{\varphi(m)}$, where $E_N:=\hbar\sum_{j=1}^d\omega_j(n_j+\frac12)$. Then $H$ is self-adjoint with

$$H\psi_N=E_N\psi_N,\qquad D(H)=\Bigl\{f:\sum_N E_N^2|\langle f,\psi_N\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \sigma(H)=\overline{\{E_N:N\in\mathbb N^d\}},$$

the span of the $\psi_N$ is a core, and on that core

$$H=\sum_{j=1}^d\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_j}\partial_{x_j}^2+\frac{m_j\omega_j^2}{2}x_j^2\Bigr);$$

(d) if $\omega_1=\cdots=\omega_d=\omega$, then $\sigma(H)=\{\hbar\omega(M+\frac d2):M\in\mathbb N\}$, and the eigenvalue $\hbar\omega(M+\frac d2)$ has multiplicity

$$\bigl|\{(n_1,\dots,n_d)\in\mathbb N^d:n_1+\cdots+n_d=M\}\bigr|=\binom{M+d-1}{d-1};$$

in particular for $d=3$ the multiplicity is $(M+1)(M+2)/2$ ([[thm-stars-and-bars]]). All parameters are positive real numbers; no physical interpretation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,K$ be complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-inner-product-space]]) and let $U:H\to K$ be a bijective linear map with
$$\langle Ux,Uy\rangle_K=\langle x,y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in H .$$
Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with spectral projection-valued measure $E_T$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]), and define
$$D(T'):=U D(T),\qquad T'(Ux):=U(Tx)\quad(x\in D(T)).$$
Then:

(a) $T'$ is well defined, linear, densely defined and self-adjoint on $K$;

(b) the assignment $E(B):=U E_T(B) U^{-1}$ on Borel sets $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a regular projection-valued measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$, and it is the spectral projection-valued measure of $T'$;

(c) for every unit vector $x\in H$ the scalar laws of the two operators agree,
$$\mu^{T'}_{Ux}(B):=\|E(B)Ux\|_K^2=\|E_T(B)x\|_H^2=:\mu^{T}_x(B)\qquad(B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel});$$

(d) $\sigma(T')=\sigma(T)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

derivations.claim: [The diagonal form of $H_1$] By [F2], $(\psi_n)$ is complete orthonormal, $H_1$ has domain $\{f:\sum_nE_n^{2}|\langle f,\psi_n\rangle|^{2}<\infty\}$ and acts by $H_1f=\sum_nE_n\langle f,\psi_n\rangle\psi_n$; since $E_n=\hbar\omega(n+\frac12)$ satisfies $n^{2}\le4(n+\frac12)^{2}$ and $(n+\frac12)^{2}\le2n^{2}+\frac12$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$, the domain condition is equivalent to $\sum_nn^{2}|\langle f,\psi_n\rangle|^{2}<\infty$, and the real numbers $E_n$ are pairwise distinct positive numbers with $E_0=\hbar\omega/2$ and $E_{n+1}-E_n=\hbar\omega$. Thus $H_1$ is the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [F4] for the family $(\psi_n)$ and the eigenvalues $E_n$, and the span of $(\psi_n)$ is a core.

[Transported ladder and number operators] The map $D$ is a bijective linear isometry by [F2], and the operators $N_\psi=DND^{-1}$, $a_\psi=DaD^{-1}$, $a^\dagger_\psi=Da^\dagger D^{-1}$ have the transported domains $D(N_\psi)=D\,D(N)$, $D(a_\psi)=D\,D(a)$, $D(a^\dagger_\psi)=D\,D(a^\dagger)$; because $\psi_n=Dg_n$ and $D$ preserves the inner product, the coefficients satisfy $\langle Dx,\psi_n\rangle=\langle x,g_n\rangle$, so by [F3] $D(N_\psi)=\{f:\sum_nn^{2}|\langle f,\psi_n\rangle|^{2}<\infty\}$ and the identities of [F3] transport: $D(a_\psi a^\dagger_\psi)=D(a^\dagger_\psi a_\psi)=D(N_\psi)$, on which $a^\dagger_\psi a_\psi=N_\psi$ and $a_\psi a^\dagger_\psi=N_\psi+I$, and $N_\psi\psi_n=n\psi_n$, $a_\psi\psi_n=\sqrt n\,\psi_{n-1}$ ($n\ge1$) with $a_\psi\psi_0=0$, $a^\dagger_\psi\psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,\psi_{n+1}$. For the non-self-adjoint pair, closedness and the adjoint relations transport by the direct pairing computation: for $x\in D(a_\psi)$ and $y\in D(a^\dagger_\psi)$, $\langle a_\psi x,y\rangle=\langle aD^{-1}x,D^{-1}y\rangle=\langle D^{-1}x,a^\dagger D^{-1}y\rangle=\langle x,a^\dagger_\psi y\rangle$, so $a_\psi\subseteq(a^\dagger_\psi)^{*}$ and $a^\dagger_\psi\subseteq a_\psi^{*}$; and if $x_k\to x$ with $a_\psi x_k\to y$, then $D^{-1}x_k\to D^{-1}x$ and $aD^{-1}x_k=D^{-1}a_\psi x_k\to D^{-1}y$, so closedness of $a$ gives $D^{-1}x\in D(a)$ and $aD^{-1}x=D^{-1}y$, that is $x\in D(a_\psi)$ and $a_\psi x=y$: $a_\psi$ is closed, and the same argument with $a^\dagger$ makes $a^\dagger_\psi$ closed. By [F8], for $y\in\mathcal H_1$, the functional $x\mapsto\langle a_\psi x,y\rangle=\langle aD^{-1}x,D^{-1}y\rangle$ on $D(a_\psi)$ is bounded in the ambient norm exactly when $D^{-1}y\in D(a^*)=D(a^\dagger)$, because $D$ is a surjective isometry between the domains. Thus $D(a_\psi^*)=D\,D(a^\dagger)$ and $a_\psi^*y=Da^*D^{-1}y=a^\dagger_\psi y$; interchanging $a$ and $a^\dagger$ proves the other adjoint equality. By [F7] applied with $U=D$ and $T=N$, the operator $N_\psi$ is self-adjoint with $\sigma(N_\psi)=\sigma(N)=\mathbb N$ and $\mu^{N_\psi}_{Dx}(B)=\mu^{N}_x(B)$ for every unit $x$ and Borel $B$.

[The three-dimensional realization] By [F6] the spectrum of $H_3$ is $\{\hbar\omega(M+\frac32)\}=\{E^{(3)}_M:M\in\mathbb N\}$, the eigenspace at $E^{(3)}_M$ has the orthonormal basis $\{\psi_N:n_1+n_2+n_3=M\}$ and dimension $(M+1)(M+2)/2$, and the least eigenvalue is $\frac32\hbar\omega$; this is clause (d), whose self-adjointness, domain and core assertions are those of [F6].

[Spectrum and eigenspaces of $H_1$] By step 1.1 the operator $H_1$ is the diagonal operator of [F4] with the pairwise distinct eigenvalues $E_n$, and by [F2] its spectrum is $\{E_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$, a closed discrete set whose least element is $E_0$ and whose consecutive gaps are $\hbar\omega$; [F4] gives $\ker(H_1-E_nI)=\mathbb C\psi_n$ for every $n$, and [F2] gives that $(\psi_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family and a core. This is clause (a).

[Number-operator identity] By steps 1.1 and 1.2, $D(H_1)=\{f:\sum_nn^{2}|\langle f,\psi_n\rangle|^{2}<\infty\}=D(N_\psi)$ and both operators act diagonally on the family, with $H_1$ having eigenvalues $E_n=\hbar\omega(n+\frac12)$ and $N_\psi$ having eigenvalues $n$; hence $H_1=\hbar\omega(N_\psi+\frac12I)$ with common domain $D(H_1)=D(N_\psi)$. By step 1.2 and [F4] the eigenspaces of $N_\psi$ are $\ker(N_\psi-nI)=\mathbb C\psi_n$, so its eigenvectors are exactly the nonzero multiples of the $\psi_n$, and its spectrum is $\mathbb N$ by [F7]. For the preparation of the unit eigenvector $\psi_n$, [F5] and the eigenspace identity give $\mu^{N_\psi}_{\psi_n}(\{n\})=\|E_{N_\psi}(\{n\})\psi_n\|^{2}=\|\psi_n\|^{2}=1$; since the scalar law of a pure preparation is a probability measure [F5], the law is the point mass $\delta_n$. Together with the ladder actions of step 1.2 this is clause (b).

[Atoms of the energy law] By [F1], $(H_1,\mathrm J)$ is an assigned sharp observable of the model whose outcome law in the pure preparation of a unit vector $f$ is $\mu^{H_1}_f(B)=\|E_{H_1}(B)f\|^{2}$. For every $n$, [F4] and step 2.1 give $\ker(H_1-E_nI)=\mathbb C\psi_n$, so the orthogonal projection $E_{H_1}(\{E_n\})$ is the projection onto $\mathbb C\psi_n$ by the first clause of [F5]; for a unit $f$ this gives $\mu^{H_1}_f(\{E_n\})=\|E_{H_1}(\{E_n\})f\|^{2}=|\langle f,\psi_n\rangle|^{2}$.

[The full law and its support] Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ be Borel. By the support clause of [F5], $\mu^{H_1}_f(B)=\mu^{H_1}_f(B\cap\sigma(H_1))$ and $\mu^{H_1}_f(\sigma(H_1))=1$; by step 2.1, $\sigma(H_1)=\{E_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$, so $B\cap\sigma(H_1)$ is the countable union of the disjoint singletons $\{E_n\}$ with $E_n\in B$, and countable additivity of the probability measure $\mu^{H_1}_f$ gives $\mu^{H_1}_f(B)=\sum_{n:E_n\in B}\mu^{H_1}_f(\{E_n\})=\sum_{n:E_n\in B}|\langle f,\psi_n\rangle|^{2}$ by step 3.1. In particular the law has no mass on Borel sets disjoint from $\{E_n\}$, and $E_n$ is an atom of the law of $f$ exactly when $\langle f,\psi_n\rangle\ne0$. This is clause (c).

[Status] Clauses (a), (b) and (c) were obtained from the postulates, the adopted model, the scaling theorem, the closed ladder operators and the general spectral law facts; clause (d) from the multidimensional theorem. No measured spectral line, no numerical value of $m$, $\omega$ or $\hbar$, no apparatus model, no selection rule and no transition rate entered, and the identification of a laboratory resonance with an eigenvalue difference is a tested identification under P7, not a consequence of the argument. This is clause (e).

boundaries.evidence: Step 4.1 writes $B\cap\sigma(H_1)$ as the countable union of the singletons $\{E_n\}$ with $E_n\in B$; for $B\cap\sigma(H_1)=\varnothing$ this is the empty union and countable additivity gives $\mu^{H_1}_f(B)=0$.
Step 3.1 gives $\mu^{H_1}_f(\{E_n\})=|\langle f,\psi_n\rangle|^{2}$, which is $0$ for an orthogonal $f$; no step divides by $\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$ or by $n$.
Steps 2.2 and 3.1 are uniform in $n$, so the single-eigenstate preparation $f=\psi_n$ and the single level $E_n$ are covered; the $n=0$ case appears explicitly in step 1.1 with $E_0=\hbar\omega/2$.

In one dimension $E_m\ne E_n$ for $m\ne n$ since $\omega>0$ (step 1.1) and step 2.1 gives one-dimensional eigenspaces; step 1.3 covers the genuinely degenerate three-dimensional levels $E^{(3)}_M$ with multiplicity $(M+1)(M+2)/2$.

Step 2.1 records the least spectral value $E_0=\hbar\omega/2$ and the gap $E_{n+1}-E_n=\hbar\omega$; the spectrum has no greatest element and no continuous endpoint, and step 4.1 evaluates the law at arbitrary Borel sets including unbounded ones.
The Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice are assumed in the statement and used through [F2], [F4], [F5] and [F7]; steps 1.1-4.1 invoke no further choice.
Step 3.1 with step 4.1: if $E_n$ is an atom of the law $\mu^{H_1}_f$, then $\mu^{H_1}_f(\{E_n\})=|\langle f,\psi_n\rangle|^{2}>0$, so $\langle f,\psi_n\rangle\ne0$.
Step 3.1: if $\langle f,\psi_n\rangle\ne0$ then $\mu^{H_1}_f(\{E_n\})=|\langle f,\psi_n\rangle|^{2}>0$, so $E_n$ is an atom of the law of $f$.

risk_review.notes: All eight steps and exact scaling, ladder, diagonal-eigenspace, multidimensional, atoms, support and Born-law suppliers reviewed. Positive parameters make the energy weights equivalent to n^2 plus the ordinary norm, including n=0. One-dimensional eigenspaces are scalar rays; finite three-dimensional level count is (M+1)(M+2)/2. Atomic probabilities sum on the discrete support for arbitrary unit f, including vectors outside D(H1). Reader scalar-multiple correction accepted. Amended the adjoint proof: closedness alone does not force equality of adjoint inclusions; ambient-norm boundedness under the unitary gives both adjoint domains and actions exactly. No empirical inputs or new Choice use.
